title: The teacher's send-off
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: a promise at the start, and a send-off at the end: let your teacher be a god to you
carry: honor mother, father, teacher, guest as god
tomorrow: five years done. so where did the whole thing begin?
last: LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.

cards: I'll call you back. I'll be there. I'll finish it this weekend.

Promises in the future tense are easy to send and easy to forget. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens its first part with a chant full of them. When that part ends, the same chant comes back, almost word for word.
Almost: the tense has changed. And just before it returns, the teacher says goodbye to his students.

teach.b: The chant is known by its first words, sham no mitrah. It asks Mitra, Varuna, Indra, Brihaspati and wide-striding Vishnu to be kind, honors Vayu, the wind, as Brahman made visible, and promises: I will speak the right.
I will speak the true. Then comes the study. And at the end of that part, the teacher sends his students home.
Speak the truth. Live by dharma. Don't neglect your study.
And then four lines many Hindus still know by heart.
Matri devo bhava: let your mother be a god to you. Pitri devo bhava: your father. Acharya devo bhava: your teacher.
Atithi devo bhava: your guest. Give with faith; give with modesty. Then the chant returns, now in the past tense.
I have spoken the true. That has protected me.

teach.h: LET YOUR TEACHER BE A GOD TO YOU.
teach.b: Om, peace, peace, peace. Here's why it matters. Many Hindu families point to these lines for habits at home: children bow to parents and teachers, often touching their feet, and a guest is welcomed like a god.
Many teachers read it this way: the Brahman the student studied is met again at home, in the people who raised him, taught him, and knock at his door. The promise is kept, and then the thanks.

how: Sham no mitrah is chanted at the opening of the Taittiriya Upanishad's first part (the Shiksha Valli), and its past-tense form is chanted when that part is finished. The teacher's send-off just before it (satyam vada, dharmam chara; matri devo bhava…) is widely memorized, and many Hindu children bow to or touch the feet of parents, elders and teachers.

games.q: what does “then two weeks of the peace chants” mean?
o: a vow to say nothing until study is over
a teacher's send-off: let your mother, father, teacher and guest be gods to you
a hymn asking for rain and a good harvest

games.q: the send-off and the chant. tap the pairs.
p: let your teacher be a god to you
let your guest be a god to you

s: the chant at the end of the Taittiriya's first part is a brand-new prayer
it's the opening chant again, with 'I will' turned into 'I have'.
the teacher's send-off asks students to honor mother, father, teacher and guest as gods
matri, pitri, acharya, atithi devo bhava: Taittiriya 1.11.
sham no mitrah honors the wind, Vayu, as Brahman made visible
honor to you, Vayu; you are Brahman made visible.

games.q: a guest drops by at dinner, and your grandmother sets the first plate in front of them before anyone eats. your friend asks why. what fits?
o: atithi devo bhava: the Taittiriya's send-off says let your guest be a god to you.
it's only politeness; there's no teaching behind it.
it's a rule that the family must always eat last, every day.
games.why: the send-off at the end of the Taittiriya's first part names four to honor as god: mother, father, teacher, guest.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher, anyone who taught you something that stuck. If you pray, fold your hands and bow your head, the way many Hindu students greet a teacher. If you don't, simply hold their face in mind.
Silently name one thing they gave you, and let each slow breath be part of that thanks.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants, and today sham no mitrah: I will speak the true at the start, I have spoken the true at the end, and between them, let your teacher be a god to you.

orig.note: Sanskrit: may Mitra be kind to us; the first words of the Taittiriya's opening chant.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: honor mother, father, teacher, guest as god. The great sayings, done.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.1 (sham no mitrah … ritam vadishyami, satyam vadishyami …), 1.11 (satyam vada, dharmam chara, svadhyayan ma pramadah … matridevo bhava, pitridevo bhava, acharyadevo bhava, atithidevo bhava … shraddhaya deyam … hriya deyam) and 1.12 (… ritam avadisham, satyam avadisham, tan mam avit …)
